subtype: Shy, embarrassed and ashamed in adult settings [Regulating]
passage: In Gothenburg, Oskar mixed up two client names in front of the whole department, and someone laughed. His face flushed, and for the rest of the meeting he spoke only when asked. At lunch he took his sandwich to a quiet corner. Sofia, from the next desk, sat down anyway and said, "Last month I called the CEO by the wrong first name. In an email." Oskar blinked and gave a small smile. She added, "Tomorrow, would you like to go over the next slide together before the call?" He nodded slowly. The next day he said just one line in the meeting, about the deadline, and his voice shook only slightly. It was a small step. By Friday he had asked a question.

qa.q: What did Oskar mix up?
qa.a: Two client names.

qa.q: What was Oskar feeling for the rest of the meeting?
qa.a: Embarrassed and ashamed, since his face flushed and he spoke only when asked.

qa.q: What small step helped Oskar?
qa.a: Speaking one line the next day, after preparing with Sofia.

qa.q: How might Sofia's story about the wrong first name help Oskar?
qa.a: It shows that public mistakes happen to others too, so his feels more ordinary. 🙂

grounding: A young adult withdraws after a public mistake, and a supportive colleague treats it as ordinary and helps him take small steps.

subtype: Shy, embarrassed and ashamed in adult settings [Regulating]
passage: At the cricket club's Sunday nets, Pooja dropped an easy catch in the practice match while the whole club watched. Someone groaned. Her ears burned, and she turned away and spent the second half fielding at the boundary, far from everyone. In the changing room she said she might skip next week. Vasudha, the senior player, sat down and said, "Everyone drops the easy ones. I dropped one in a league match last year, in front of my parents." She didn't tell Pooja not to feel bad. She asked, "Want to do ten catches with me before nets next week? Just us." Pooja hesitated, then nodded. The next Sunday, after catching seven of ten, she asked to stand at slip.

qa.q: Where did Pooja field in the second half?
qa.a: At the boundary, far from everyone.

qa.q: What was Pooja feeling after she dropped the catch?
qa.a: Embarrassed and ashamed, since her ears burned, she pulled away and she considered skipping next week.

qa.q: How did Vasudha help Pooja return?
qa.a: She shared her own dropped catch, offered private practice and a small step.

qa.q: How might the club see the dropped catch?
qa.a: As an ordinary slip, since Vasudha says everyone drops the easy ones; the groan was probably a passing reaction.

grounding: A young adult withdraws after a public mistake at a club, and a supportive senior treats it as ordinary and offers a small private step.

subtype: Shy, embarrassed and ashamed in adult settings [Regulating]
passage:
Dear Madhav,
You asked why I've been so quiet in meetings since the client presentation. Honestly, I've been hiding.
You remember: I called Mrs. Chakraborty "Mrs. Chatterjee" three times in front of her whole board, and someone laughed. I went red, lost my place, and finished the slides in a whisper. Since then I've been blushing every time I have to speak, even in our small team calls. I keep replaying it in the shower.
Last week I told my sister, and she said, "Wasim, everyone has one of those. You're not the first person to mix up a name." It helped more than I expected, just saying it out loud.
So I've made myself a small plan. This week, one comment in the Monday call. Next week, I'll present the timeline slide. I've even practised Mrs. Chakraborty's name in the mirror twenty times.
If you see me go red on Monday, just nod at me.
Wasim

qa.q: What name did Wasim wrongly call Mrs. Chakraborty?
qa.a: 'Mrs. Chatterjee'.

qa.q: How has Wasim been feeling since the presentation?
qa.a: Wasim has felt embarrassed and ashamed, blushing whenever speaking and replaying the moment.

qa.q: What small steps is Wasim taking to loosen the shame?
qa.a: Talking to a supportive sister, treating the mistake as ordinary, and planning small exposures: one comment in the Monday call, then presenting the timeline slide.

qa.q: How did Wasim's sister help?
qa.a: She treated the mistake as ordinary, saying everyone has one of those, which made it easier for Wasim to say it out loud.

grounding: Shows a young professional withdrawing and blushing after a public mistake, and using support and small exposures to reduce shame.

subtype: Shy, embarrassed and ashamed in adult settings [Regulating]
passage: My most embarrassing moment, Hafsa? Easy. My first all-hands at the bank, I was asked to share our team's results. I walked up, tripped on the mic cable, and landed on my knees in front of three hundred people. Someone laughed, then everyone did. I got up, said two sentences, and fled. For a month after that I didn't say a word in any meeting. I ate lunch at my desk. I'd go red if anyone even said "cable". Then my manager, Leela, took me for coffee and told me she'd once spilt tea on the chief executive. "Ordinary disaster," she said. "Survivable." She asked me to do small things: first a one-line update in a team meeting, then a five-minute talk to six people. Each one was a little easier. Last month I spoke at the all-hands again. I stepped over the cable, very deliberately, and got a laugh on purpose. I'm Shankar, and I'm still slightly scared of cables.

qa.q: How many people were at the all-hands?
qa.a: Three hundred people.

qa.q: How did Shankar feel in the month after the fall?
qa.a: Shankar felt ashamed and embarrassed, going red at the word 'cable' and avoiding speaking in meetings.

qa.q: What helped Shankar recover from the shame?
qa.a: Leela treating it as an ordinary disaster, sharing her own, and guiding small exposures from a one-line update to a short talk, until the all-hands again.

qa.q: How did Leela see Shankar's fall?
qa.a: Leela saw it as an 'ordinary disaster', survivable, like her own tea spill on the chief executive.

grounding: A young professional describes withdrawing after a public fall and recovering through a supportive manager and small exposures.

subtype: Shy, embarrassed and ashamed in adult settings [Regulating]
passage: I'm Chaitanya, and I sit two rows from Ira. On Tuesday she meant to send her sister a message about their mother's birthday cake, and sent it to the whole company list instead: "Make sure it's chocolate, Ma hates the vanilla one from last year." Four hundred people. Within minutes people were replying with cake pictures. Ira went bright red, and for the rest of the week she barely looked up. She stopped coming to the lunch table. In the team meeting she said nothing at all. I couldn't tell whether she was mortified or just keeping her head down. On Friday our lead, Radhika, told the whole team about the time she'd emailed her own salary slip to a client, and we all groaned and laughed. Then someone asked Ira, "So, did your mother get chocolate?" Ira hesitated, then laughed too. "Chocolate. She loved it." The next week she came back to the lunch table. The week after, she presented the monthly report.

qa.q: How many people received Ira's message?
qa.a: Four hundred people.

qa.q: What might Ira have been feeling during that week?
qa.a: Ira was probably mortified and ashamed, going red and withdrawing, though Chaitanya couldn't be sure if she was just keeping her head down.

qa.q: What helped Ira come back?
qa.a: Radhika sharing her own email mistake made it ordinary, and a friendly question let Ira laugh; then she returned to lunch and later presented the report, step by step.

qa.q: How did Radhika help the team respond?
qa.a: By telling her own embarrassing email story, Radhika made mistakes feel normal and invited laughter with Ira rather than at her.

grounding: An observer describes a young professional withdrawing after a public email mistake and supportive colleagues making it ordinary.

passage:
Monday: Pranav's microphone squealed during the quarterly town hall, and in the scramble he called the finance head by the wrong name. A ripple of laughter went round the room. His ears burned for the rest of the day, and at lunch he carried his dal-rice to his desk instead of the canteen.
Thursday: In the team huddle he kept his camera off and typed "agree" in the chat rather than speak. Gurleen messaged him afterwards: "I once called our CEO 'Mummy' in a review 😅 Nobody remembers. Chai at four?" Over chai she told the whole story, and he laughed for the first time that week.
The next Tuesday: Pranav asked one question in the smaller design review. His voice wobbled, but nobody looked up oddly. On Friday he gave a three-minute update, stumbled once, said "let me try that again," and carried on.

qa.q: What did Pranav type in the huddle chat instead of speaking?
qa.a: Pranav typed "agree" in the chat.

qa.q: What do Pranav's burning ears and lunch at his desk suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: Most likely embarrassment and shame after the laughter, though he might also have just wanted quiet to recover from a stressful morning.

qa.q: What small step would help someone like Pranav after a public mistake?
qa.a: Starting with one question in a smaller meeting, as Pranav did, lets the fear shrink before a bigger task like a full update.

qa.q: Why might Gurleen have shared her own embarrassing story?
qa.a: Gurleen probably wanted Pranav to see his slip as ordinary; showing she had lived through something similar made it easier for him to laugh 😊

grounding: Shows a young adult withdrawing after a public mistake and easing shame through a supportive colleague and small, gradual steps.
